scene.note: Imran sets the price, the leak limit and the company's key on the laptop, and your scripts read them when they run instead of keeping them in their code.

steps.note: In April, Imran sets this year's water price in the laptop's settings, not in the code.
water-bill.js reads the price each time it runs, and the litres typed after its name.
The cost of the litres shows on the screen, or one plain line says the price is not set.
Someone types the price by hand, and sometimes it comes out as a word, with a comma, or empty.
water-bill.js turns the setting into a number and decides whether that number is a price.
A price that is not one is refused with one line that names the setting, and no bill is worked out.
water-bill.js reads the leak limit too. When nobody set it, or it is empty, the script uses its own default.
It works out the bill as before, then compares the litres with the limit, as numbers.
Above the limit, a warning to check the taps comes on standard error, beside the bill.
The water company's account key sits in the laptop's settings with the others.
settings.js looks at the three settings the water scripts use, and only at those.
The screen shows the price, the limit and whether the key is set. The key itself never shows.
